JOURNAL OF L ATEX CLASS FILES, VOL. 14, NO. 8, AUGUST 2025 1
Interacting Multiple Model Proprioceptive
Odometry for Legged Robots
Wanlei Li, Zichang Chen, Shilei Li, Xiaogang Xiong, Yunjiang Lou .
Abstract—State estimation for legged robots remains chal-
lenging because legged odometry generally suffers from limited
observability and therefore depends critically on measurement
constraints to suppress drift. When exteroceptive sensors are
unreliable or degraded, such constraints are mainly derived
from proprioceptive measurements, particularly leg kinematics
and contact information. However, most existing proprioceptive
odometry methods rely on an idealized point-contact assumption,
which is often violated during real locomotion on complex terrain.
Consequently, the effectiveness of proprioceptive constraints may
be significantly reduced, resulting in degraded estimation accu-
racy. To address these limitations, we propose an interacting mul-
tiple model (IMM)-based proprioceptive odometry framework
for legged robots. By incorporating multiple contact hypotheses
within a unified probabilistic framework, the proposed method
enables online mode switching and probabilistic fusion under
varying contact conditions. Extensive simulations and real-world
experiments demonstrate that the proposed method achieves
superior pose estimation accuracy over state-of-the-art methods
while maintaining comparable computational efficiency.
Index Terms—Legged Robots, Proprioceptive Sensors, Inter-
acting Multiple Model.
I. INTRODUCTION
LEGGED robots have been widely deployed in complex
and unstructured environments due to their ability to
traverse uneven terrain. To achieve reliable locomotion in such
environments, accurate state estimation is essential. Conse-
quently, a wide range of state estimation algorithms have been
developed using different sensing modalities [1]–[5]. These ap-
proaches typically rely on either proprioceptive sensors, such
as inertial measurement units (IMU), joint encoders, torque
and force sensors, or exteroceptive sensors, including cameras,
LiDAR, and global positioning systems (GPS) systems.
Although fusing proprioceptive and exteroceptive sensors
can significantly improve estimation accuracy, exteroceptive
measurements are often degraded or unavailable in real-world
scenarios. For example, vision-based sensors are sensitive to
reflective or transparent surfaces, lighting variations, motion
blur, and environmental occlusions. These limitations motivate
the development of state estimation methods that rely solely
on proprioceptive sensing, which provides a robust baseline
when exteroceptive information is absent or corrupted.

based methods [4], [8] are particularly attractive for real-
time legged locomotion because they offer a favorable balance
between estimation accuracy and computational efficiency.
However, their effectiveness depends strongly on the validity
of the assumed foot-ground contact model.
Most existing proprioceptive odometry methods rely on
a static point-contact assumption. In practice, foot-ground
interactions are often non-ideal and time-varying under com-
plex terrain conditions. The robot foot may deviate from
the idealized point-contact behavior, and slippage may occur
under insufficient friction or external disturbances. As a re-
sult, the proprioceptive constraints constructed from a single
fixed contact model become unreliable, significantly degrading
estimation accuracy. These limitations motivate the use of a
multiple-hypothesis estimation framework that can infer and
fuse different contact conditions in a unified probabilistic
manner.
To address these challenges, this paper proposes an inter-
acting multiple model (IMM)-based proprioceptive odometry
framework for legged robots. The proposed method enables
online inference and probabilistic fusion of multiple contact
hypotheses under varying foot-ground interaction conditions.
In addition, a rolling-aware estimation design is introduced by
incorporating foot velocity into the estimator state, allowing
the estimator to better account for contact-induced motion
deviations using only proprioceptive sensing. The main con-
tributions of this work are summarized as follows:
•We formulate proprioceptive odometry for legged robots
under dynamic foot–ground interaction as a multiple-
contact hypothesis estimation problem, and develop an
IMM-based filtering framework for online contact-mode
inference and fusion.
•We propose a rolling-aware state augmentation by incor-
porating foot velocity into the estimator state, enabling
explicit modeling of contact-induced motion deviations
using only proprioceptive measurements.
•Extensive simulations and real-world experiments demon-
strate that the proposed rolling-aware multi-model esti-
mator improves accuracy and robustness under slippery
and challenging contact conditions, while outperform-
ing state-of-the-art proprioceptive methods at comparable

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Sec. II
reviews related work; Sec. III introduces the proposed propri-

II. RELATEDWORK
For legged robot state estimation, a widely adopted ap-
proach is to fuse inertial and kinematic information using low-
cost proprioceptive sensors such as IMU and joint encoders.
In this context, proprioceptive odometry (PO) has emerged
as a dominant paradigm, enabling continuous state estimation
using only inertial and kinematic measurements. For example,
Bloesch et al. [8] proposed an Extended Kalman filter (EKF)-
based state estimator for quadruped robots, which incorporates
leg kinematics and contact constraints into the observation
model. This framework was later implemented on the MIT
Cheetah 3 robot using a linear Kalman filter formulation [9].
Although these approaches demonstrate observability of the
body position, velocity, roll, and pitch, their convergence may
be slow due to linearization errors and mismatched error
distributions. Hartley et al. [4] later reformulated the estimator
as an invariant extended Kalman filter (IEKF), deriving the
estimation equations directly on the Lie group manifold and
significantly improving consistency and convergence proper-
ties. More recently, similar estimation principles have been
extended to learning-based approaches [6], [7]. However, such
methods typically rely on large-scale training datasets and lack
guaranteed robustness in previously unseen scenarios.
To enhance robustness and long-term accuracy, another
line of research introduces exteroceptive sensors, such as
cameras and LiDAR, which provide additional environmen-
tal constraints. For example, Wisth et al. [1] developed a
tightly coupled visual–inertial–leg odometry system based on
factor graphs, incorporating kinematic velocity measurements.
In subsequent work [2], LiDAR sensing was further inte-
grated into the framework, enabling reliable state estimation
across diverse and challenging terrains. However, as mentioned
above, these exteroceptive sensors may be sensitive to environ-
mental conditions in degenerate scenarios, potentially leading
to decreased accuracy or even complete failure in challenging
environments. As a result, purely proprioceptive state estima-
tion remains an essential and indispensable solution for legged
robots operating in such conditions.
However, kinematic–inertial methods based solely on pro-
prioceptive sensing typically assume that the contact location
of a stance foot remains static throughout the stance phase.
This assumption is often violated in practice due to dynamic
foot–ground contact, leading to link deformation and slippage,
which are major sources of leg odometry drift [10]. To
address errors induced by link deformation, several works
explicitly account for kinematic model uncertainties within
the estimation framework. For instance, Agrawal et al. [11]
incorporated uncertainty in the kinematic chain to reduce
estimation errors caused by structural deformation. Similarly,
[12] proposed an online link calibration approach to mitigate
positional drift arising from time-varying kinematic parameters
under dynamic contact conditions.In addition to link deformation, foot–ground slip further
violates the static contact assumption and degrades state es-
timation accuracy. To mitigate this issue, Bloesch et al. [3]
proposed a UKF that fuses IMU and kinematic velocity
measurements, where a Mahalanobis-distance threshold on the
filter innovation is used to reject unreliable velocity observa-
tions. This idea was later extended by Kim et al. [13], who
instead used a tunable threshold on the estimated contact foot
velocity. Wisth et al. [2] modeled dynamic contact as a bias
term in the linear velocity measurement from leg odometry.
Yang et al. [14] further investigated rolling contact effects by
embedding multiple IMUs along the leg to measure the an-
gular velocity induced by foot rolling, although this approach
requires additional sensing hardware. To handle systems with
switching dynamics, the interacting multiple model (IMM)
framework has been widely applied in robotics and other
dynamic systems [15], [16]. By maintaining multiple candidate
models and recursively updating their posterior probabilities
online, IMM enables effective adaptation to time-varying
system behaviors. However, such multi-model strategies have
rarely been explored in proprioceptive odometry for legged
robots, where foot-ground interaction conditions may switch
among different contact modes. Despite recent advances, most
existing methods still rely on heuristic thresholds, single-
model assumptions, or additional sensing to handle contact-
induced disturbances, without explicitly modeling multiple
contact modes within a unified probabilistic framework.

update. We then extend this estimator to an IMM framework,
where different contact conditions, especially slippage, are
captured through mode-dependent foot velocity uncertainty.

Remark 3.Although the proposed IMM framework can in
principle accommodate more contact modes, these additional
modes mainly correspond to a finer discretization of the noise
scale. In practice, however, closely related modes may not
be reliably distinguishable from the available proprioceptive
measurements, while increasing the number of modes also
leads to higher computational cost. Therefore, a two-mode
realization is adopted in this work, consisting of a nominal
rolling mode and a slip mode with inflated foot velocity noise,
which is generally sufficient for practical applications.
IV. EXPERIMENTS
To evaluate the performance of the proposed framework,
experiments were conducted in both simulations and real-
world settings using the AlienGo quadruped robot under a
trot gait. The robot integrates IMUs and joint encoders. The
open-source Pinocchio library [19] was utilized to model the
kinematics of the legged robot.
To evaluate the proposed framework, we compared IMM-
PO with several representative baselines, including the KF
[9], ESKF [8], invariant extended Kalman filter (IEKF) [4],
ESKF-VB [20], KalmanNet [21], and ESKF-R, which denotes
the single-model rolling-aware ESKF without IMM-based
mode adaptation. ESKF-VB employs a variational Bayesian
scheme to account for time-varying process noise covariance,

D. Detailed Analysis of the KalmanNet Baseline
To better understand the behavior of the learning-based
baseline, we provide additional implementation details and
error analysis for KalmanNet. In our task, quadruped pro-
prioceptive state estimation involves high-dimensional and
strongly coupled dynamics together with time-varying foot-
ground interactions. Under such conditions, directly apply-
ing the standard KalmanNet training pipeline yields limited
training and testing performance, suggesting that the original
formulation is insufficient for this challenging setting.
KalmanNet employs a two-layer recurrent neural network
to estimate the Kalman gain from filtering-related features,
rather than directly regressing the robot state. While this design
preserves the recursive correction structure of the Kalman
filter, it also makes the update quality strongly dependent
on the recurrent hidden state. In quadruped proprioceptive
odometry, the estimator must cope with long-horizon tempo-
ral dependencies, contact-mode transitions, and time-varying
disturbances. Under these conditions, a compact recurrentrepresentation may be insufficient to fully capture the complex
evolution of foot–ground interaction, leading to biased gain
prediction and degraded closed-loop stability, especially on
long real-world trajectories. More importantly, unlike model-
based estimators with explicit mode-dependent contact un-
certainty, KalmanNet adapts the correction implicitly through
learned recurrent features, which limits its robustness when
rolling and slipping behaviors alternate over time.

several training enhancements were introduced, including pla-

strategies enlarge the effective data coverage and improve

addition to the standard position and attitude losses, we further

To further alleviate the training difficulty associated with
long recursive horizons, curriculum learning was adopted by
progressively increasing the sequence length during training.
This strategy allows the network to first learn short-term
correction behavior and local dynamics before handling more
challenging long-range temporal dependencies. In addition, a
learning-rate scheduling strategy with a prescribed minimum
threshold was employed to reduce optimization oscillation and
mitigate occasional training collapse when the sequence length
becomes large. The difficulty of long-sequence learning is
not only due to deeper temporal recursion, but also due to
the coupling between gain prediction and state evolution: an
inaccurate gain at an early stage perturbs the subsequent state
estimate, which in turn changes later network inputs and may
further amplify the deviation.
The training configuration is as follows. The network is a
two-layer LSTM with hidden size 512 and dropout 0.1. The
maximum sequence length is 1440, the curriculum step is 16,
the batch size is 8, and each curriculum stage is trained for
100 epochs, followed by 1000 post-training epochs on the full
sequence length. AdamW is used with an initial learning rate
of 3×10−4, weight decay 10−2, StepLR decay factor 0.999,
and minimum learning rate 2×10−5. The loss weights are
λp=1,λ r=10−2, andλ e=10−6, and the random seed is

33607.007 s, which is approximately 9.34 h.

V. CONCLUSIONS
This paper presented an IMM-based proprioceptive odome-
try for legged robots under dynamic foot-ground interactions.
Unlike conventional point-contact formulations, the proposed
method distinguishes rolling-induced structured contact mo-
tion from slip-induced uncertainty. Specifically, a rolling-
aware ESKF was developed by augmenting the foot velocity
in the state and introducing a rolling-consistent kinematic
update, and was further integrated into an IMM framework
for online adaptation of contact confidence through mode-
dependent foot velocity uncertainty. The proposed framework
was validated in both simulation and real-world experiments.
The results show that explicit rolling modeling reduces the bias
caused by the conventional zero-velocity contact assumption,
while IMM-based multi-model inference improves robustness
under slip and uncertain terrain interactions. Overall, the
proposed estimator consistently outperformed representative
proprioceptive baselines under challenging contact conditions
with comparable computational cost.

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces an Interacting Multiple Model (IMM)-based proprioceptive odometry framework for legged robots. The main points covered are:

*   **Problem Statement:** Existing proprioceptive odometry methods for legged robots often rely on an idealized point-contact assumption, which is frequently violated in real-world scenarios with complex terrain. This violation leads to degraded estimation accuracy, especially when exteroceptive sensors are unreliable.
*   **Proposed Solution:** The paper proposes an IMM-based framework that incorporates multiple contact hypotheses within a unified probabilistic framework. This allows for online mode switching and probabilistic fusion of different contact conditions.
*   **Key Innovations:**
    *   Formulation of proprioceptive odometry under dynamic foot-ground interaction as a multiple-contact hypothesis estimation problem.
    *   Development of an IMM-based filtering framework for online contact-mode inference and fusion.

structure.title: IMM Framework
structure.summary:
The document describes a rolling-aware proprioceptive state estimator for legged robots, utilizing an Interacting Multiple Model (IMM) framework. The core of the estimator involves a prediction step and an update step, both of which are mode-conditioned.

The **prediction step** uses a shared nominal propagation model across all contact modes. This model describes the robot's dynamics, including position, velocity, orientation, and biases, and incorporates IMU measurements. The process noise statistics, particularly for foot velocity, differ between modes to reflect distinct contact conditions. The prediction involves propagating the state and its covariance using discrete-time transition matrices and process noise covariances derived from continuous-time dynamics.

The **update step** incorporates kinematic measurements from joint encoders. It contrasts a conventional point-contact model, which assumes a stationary stance foot, with a proposed rolling-aware measurement model. The rolling-aware model explicitly accounts for deterministic non-zero velocity of the contact point due to rolling by augmenting the state with foot-end velocity and introducing rolling-consistent constraints. This model is designed to mitigate modeling bias and improve estimation consistency during the stance phase, especially when rolling occurs.

The **IMM framework** embeds the rolling-aware Extended State Kalman Filter (ESKF) into an IMM structure. Different contact modes are distinguished by varying process noise levels associated with foot velocity, rather than different measurement functions. This approach captures the effect of slippage by enlarging the foot velocity process noise covariance, reflecting weakened constraint confidence. The IMM framework involves mixing posterior estimates from previous steps, predicting mode probabilities, and then fusing the mode-conditioned estimates to obtain a final posterior estimate. The document suggests a two-mode realization (nominal rolling and slip) as a practical approach.

The document also outlines the **experimental setup** for evaluating the proposed framework. This includes simulations in Gazebo across various scenarios (flat surface, slippery, uneven terrain, slope) and real-world experiments with the AlienGo quadruped robot. The proposed method (IMM-PO) is compared against several baselines, including KF, ESKF, IEKF, ESKF-VB, KalmanNet, and a single-model rolling-aware ESKF (ESKF-R). Performance is assessed using Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE) and Relative Pose Error (RPE) metrics.

structure.title: CONCLUSIONS
structure.summary:
This partial document discusses advancements in state estimation for legged robots, focusing on improving robustness and accuracy, particularly under challenging foot-ground interactions. Key points covered include:

*   **Training Strategies for Long-Sequence Learning:** The document details techniques to overcome the difficulty of training neural networks on long recursive horizons. This involves curriculum learning (progressively increasing sequence length) to first learn short-term behaviors and then long-range dependencies. A learning-rate scheduling strategy with a minimum threshold is also employed to reduce oscillations and prevent training collapse. The coupling between gain prediction and state evolution is identified as a significant challenge in long-sequence learning.
*   **Specific Training Configuration:** A detailed training configuration for a two-layer LSTM network is provided, including hidden size, dropout, maximum sequence length, curriculum step, batch size, epochs per stage, optimizer (AdamW), learning rate schedule, weight decay, loss weights, and random seed. The elapsed training time is also reported.
*   **Quantitative Results and Analysis:** Table V presents quantitative results (ATE and RPE for position and attitude) on real-world and simulated trajectories. The results highlight KalmanNet's effectiveness on short real-world segments but reveal a dramatic increase in position ATE on a longer real-world trajectory, indicating accumulated global drift despite effective local corrections. Simulated trajectories, being shorter and cleaner, show significantly lower errors.
*   **Stability Analysis:** Figure 10 illustrates the evolution of a closed-loop stability indicator (spectral radius). The document explains that a spectral radius below 1 signifies locally stable error dynamics, while values approaching or exceeding 1 indicate potential error amplification. The deterioration of this metric over time suggests increasingly unstable recursive behavior in longer trajectories.
*   **Conclusions on Model Performance:** The enhanced training strategy improves KalmanNet's robustness and generalization on short sequences. However, the significant gap between local RPE and global ATE on long real-world trajectories points to a limitation in handling long-horizon proprioceptive state estimation under complex foot-ground interactions, despite preserving short-range consistency.
*   **Proposed Framework Overview (from Conclusion):** The paper presents an IMM-based proprioceptive odometry for legged robots that distinguishes between rolling-induced structured contact motion and slip-induced uncertainty. It introduces a rolling-aware ESKF with an augmented state and a rolling-consistent kinematic update, integrated into an IMM framework for online adaptation of contact confidence. This framework is validated in simulation and real-world experiments, showing reduced bias from zero-velocity assumptions and improved robustness under slip and uncertain terrain.
